forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle schools-funding deficit forecast to reach £17.153m by March 2027, with override extended to 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle City Council expects the deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £17.153m by the end of 2026-27, according to the first-quarter outturn report (the forecast of the year's actual figures) put to Cabinet on 21 September. The grant is projecting an overspend of £11.297m this year, on top of a negative balance of £5.808m at 1 April 2026.

The overspend is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending there is forecast at £66.6m against funding of £55.2m. The paper puts spending growth at 15%, against 7% growth in funding.

For now the deficit does not touch the council's main budget. A statutory override (a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet) lets the council record it as an unusable reserve. The override was due to expire in March 2026, and the government has extended it to March 2028. The government is also offering a High Needs Stability Grant, covering up to 90% of eligible deficits, but it depends on the Department for Education approving a plan to reform support for children with special educational needs.

findings.headline: Services currently funded by levy (CCTV, Street Marshals, women's safety training) will depend on discretionary partnership funding, with women's safety organizations raising service continuity concerns
findings.detail: Levy-funded services including CCTV, Street Marshals, Taxi Marshals, Safe Haven, Shout Up (women's safety training), and cleansing will transfer to NE1-administered fund after revocation. Women's safety and violence-prevention organizations have expressed strong opposition to abolition unless sustainable replacement funding is secured, arguing that levy-funded interventions form an integrated public safety system.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders track service continuity and funding security; moving from statutory to discretionary funding creates greater risk, particularly for public safety services addressing violence against women and girls.
findings.figures: Services funded include CCTV, Street Marshals, Taxi Marshals, Safe Haven, Shout Up (training more than 4,850 staff since 2017, 65 certified venues), and cleansing
findings.quote: organisations supporting women and girls strongly oppose the abolition unless sustainable replacement funding is secured. They argue that levy-funded interventions form an integrated public safety system that reduces vulnerability and supports safer management of the night-time economy.

findings.headline: Late-night levy being revoked due to hospitality sector cost-of-living pressure; 78% of 255 consultation respondents supported abolition
findings.detail: The council is ending the levy primarily to reduce financial burden on licensed premises and hospitality businesses facing pressure from the cost-of-living crisis and increased business costs. The council views the levy as creating an unfair competitive disadvantage for Newcastle (one of only two councils outside London still charging it, alongside Liverpool). Consultation showed strong business support: 93% of city centre venues and 78% of overall respondents supported abolition.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders would want to know if councils are making revenue decisions based on economic policy grounds and how this affects financial planning and service funding.
findings.figures: 78% of 255 consultation respondents supported abolition; 93% of 65 city centre venues supported abolition (NE1 survey); Newcastle and Liverpool the only councils outside London still charging the levy
findings.quote: The hospitality sector has come under severe pressure because of the cost-of-living crisis and increased business costs making trading conditions difficult. It will assist in the viability of existing businesses but also those considering opening in the city which may by virtue of their planned opening hours be liable for the late-night levy fee.

findings.headline: Council revoking statutory late-night levy generating £216k annually and replacing with discretionary partnership funding administered by NE1
findings.detail: Newcastle is ending its late-night levy scheme introduced in 2013, which generates £216k annually (£151k to Police and Crime Commissioner, £65k retained by Council). The alternative arrangement will see NE1 (the business improvement district) establish a governance board to administer a fund at the same expected financial level, funded through voluntary contributions rather than mandatory levies on licensed premises.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender would want to understand shifts from statutory to discretionary funding models, as discretionary revenue is less certain and governance changes can affect service reliability and revenue predictability.
findings.figures: £3.46 million generated since 2013; £216k annual fund (£151k PCC, £65k Council); 78% of consultation respondents supported abolition
findings.quote: the fund is expected to be at the same financial level as the last full financial year of the levy and provide funds of £216k. (£151K to the Police and Crime Commissioner/ £65K to Newcastle City Council)

findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer confirmed adequacy of reserves for 2025/26
findings.detail: In the statutory Section 25 statement, the Chief Finance Officer confirmed both the robustness of budget estimates and the adequacy of reserves for 2025/26. The Audit and Standards Committee considered this statement and provided assurance on the adequacy of arrangements.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer finance directors monitor reserve adequacy as a buffer against financial shocks. The Section 25 statement is the statutory assurance on this.
findings.figures: none — statement of adequacy only, specific reserve levels not disclosed
findings.quote: The Committee also considered the Section 25 statement made by the Chief Finance Officer confirming the robustness of budget estimates and adequacy of reserves

findings.headline: Internal audit: substantial assurance on governance and control framework in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor's opinion was that based on audit work in 2025/26, there was substantial assurance that an effective framework of governance, risk management and control was in place. This represents the highest tier of audit assurance and indicates no significant control issues.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer finance directors monitor the internal audit opinion on control environment as a key indicator of governance strength.
findings.figures: none — assessment expressed as 'substantial assurance' (top tier of audit assurance)
findings.quote: based on the internal audit work there was substantial assurance that an effective framework of governance, risk management and control was in place in 2025/26
